The Role of Sound on Spirituality in Religious Environments
and Islamic Architecture by Using EEG
Alessandra De Cesaris1 · Ali Sadeghi habibabad1
Accepted: 25 April 2023 / Published online: 16 May 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023
Abstract
This present study aims to investigate the effects of the sound pressure level on mosque
users’ brain waves in the interior of the Nasir al-Mulk mosque in Shiraz. The research
hypothesis is based on the fact that the sound pressure level is significantly related to the
spiritual sense in the environmental psychology of the mosque. According, in the first step,
a survey method is applied, the population of experts is formed, and sound characteristics
are ranked using a questionnaire and Friedman’s test. Next, the sound pressure level, which
obtained the top rank, is selected to be tested and examined. In the second step, using a lab-
oratory method and a brain wave recording device, 6 sound intensities indices were simu-
lated and prepared in the software to carry out the test. The sound used in the present study
is “Adhan” since the case study is an Islamic mosque. The test was done in the laboratory
and a quiet room. To do the tests, the subjects were asked to sit and the sound was played
through headphones for them. The 360-degree image of the mosque was shown to the sub-
jects through virtual reality glasses, and finally, the data obtained from the brain waves
recorded by special devices are prepared for review and analysis. The general results of
the first step showed that among the characteristics of sound that are effective in creating/
enhancing the spiritual sense in the architecture of mosques, sound pressure level obtains
the highest score, followed by sound concept, the amplitude of sound, sound quality, sound
source, and sound type, respectively. Also, the general results of the analysis of users’ brain
waves in the second part showed that sound pressure level (40–45 dB) is the most effective
level in creating/enhancing a spiritual sense in the Nasir al-Mulk Mosque in Shiraz.

Introduction
Each person experiences spiritual spaces in different ways, the extent of which depends
on his innate talent, cultural perception, and past experiences. What is shared by these
characteristics is that the experiences of each person are formed inside his head and then,
modified and adjusted, and shared with others through a reaction (Edelstein, ). At the level
of architectural experience, or more specifically, human response to spaces, the nature of
space is clearly effective. The characteristics of space from form to color, thermal condi-
tions, natural and artificial light, and sound are received by our sensory systems. This pro-
cess is sent through the gray matter and midbrain to the cerebral cortex to be recognized
through a conscious pathway. All these mechanisms occur in a millionth of a second. The
brain has two primary functions that can be considered both biologically and evolutionar-
ily. These functions are self-sustaining or self-transcendence. The brain performs both of
these functions throughout our lives. On the other hand, religion also performs both of
these functions. Therefore, from the point of view of the brain, religion is a wonderful
tool, because religion helps the brain in performing its basic functions unless the human
brain suddenly makes fundamental changes in its functions (Edelstein, HYPERLINK
"sps:refid::bib35|bib36" ).
If architecture is examined in relation to religion and a place to perform religious acts,
there would be three different views on the relationship between these two. The first view
deals with the purpose of architecture and the ways that architecture expresses spirituality
through various elements and materials. The second view is the phenomenological dimen-
sion of spirituality, which includes physical experiences and emotions formed by human
interactions with architecture, and the third view is the role of cultural and social charac-
teristics of an architectural building in expressing spirituality and its ethical, relational, and
symbolic functions (Barrie & Bermudez, 2019; Danesh, 2021).
Music as an external stimulus effective on multi-sensory perception through the sense
of hearing in the architecture of mosques and religious places has been considered in many
studies. Also, in addition to examining the implicit concepts created by sound in architec-
tural components such as domes, vaults, and altars, the effect of the materials used on the
sound of music, the creation of reverberation, and how listeners in different places have the
same perception of music in line with the purpose of the religious building (Morgan, 2010;
Egner, 2003). The use of the building is very important to decide how much the reflec-
tion and reverberation of the sound will be. This issue has always been considered in reli-
gious buildings. The application of some materials can be examined from the perspective
of hearing in addition to vision. These materials reflect sound at a very high level (Danesh,
2021; Pentcheva, 2011).
The present study aims to investigate the effect of sound pressure levels on the minds of
users of religious spaces. The research hypothesis is based on the fact that in addition to the
type of sound (favorable sound, unfavorable sound), which was investigated in the author’s
previous research, the characteristics of the sound itself are involved in mental effects and
can influence people’s emotions and feelings. This has been stated in the form of theory in
previous research and it is necessary to scientifically prove it. Therefore, after identifying
the characteristics of the sound, one factor (sound pressure level) was selected to conduct
the test and it has been investigated in the case study (Nasir al-Mulk Mosque, Shiraz).

It seems that the lack of codified rules for Characteristic of sound/acoustics for reli-
gious places to promote the spiritual dimension is the main issue of the research that more
research is required in this area. The confusion of Characteristic of sound in religious
places, such as mosque’s, causes researchers to think of developing principles and rules
to study the amount of sound needed in the interior of such buildings, and based on these
principles, the quality of the interior will guide the religious places to improve the spiritual
dimension.
The contemporary architecture’s negligence of the spiritual aspects in the architectural
spaces of the religious places, especially the mosques, is an issue adversely influencing the
Islamic society and its buildings, including mosques and the other religious constructions.
With all its daily issues and concerns, architecture and urban engineering need to offer a
sort of tranquility to the people in the today’s society and make the spiritual sense flow-
ing in the architectural works and people’s lives through the use of special techniques. The
present study tries identifying the indices influencing spiritual sense in Architecture Of
Islamic Mosques thereby to more subtly investigate the Sound Pressure Level; in addition,
the study product will be eventually suggesting the most appropriate Sound Pressure Level
for religious environments like mosques and prioritization of various of Sound Pressure
Level based on the extent to which they cause the enhancement of tranquility and sense of
spirituality through analyzing the brain waves of the users of such buildings.
The study tries to examine the effect of the Sound Pressure Level on the humanbrain. It
is done using brainwave recording of the audience who are using the mosque’s architecture
(Nasir al-Mulk mosque in Shiraz, Iran).
Research Background
The goal of creating religious spaces like mosque is the recreation of a motion directing the
observers’ attentions to another world. Many indices can be mentioned with effects on the
creation of spiritual sense; these indicators and indices can be counted through an investi-
gation in the background and prior research which will be presented below; however, deal-
ing with all these indicators entails a lot of time and a huge effort hence it is beyond the
scope of a single research. Efforts have been accordingly made herein to only investigate
sound in the architectural designing of the mosques, especially the its characteristics.
So far, much research has been carried out on the acoustics and mental effects of sound
in the architecture of mosques all over the world, as generally presented in (Table 1). How-
ever, there is no research on the effectiveness of the sound pressure level in the creation/
enhancement of the spiritual sense in the architecture of mosques.
Research Literature
Architecture and Human
Human dimension in architecture and People as the End Users must be taking an important
role in every work of architecture and should not be left in the creation of works of archi-
tecture to avoid the Failure of Architecture. Architecture is a work of art and is made to fit
the needs of functional, social, cultural, technical and climate (Indriyati, 2018). Its exist-
ence is closely related to the daily rhythm of human life (Sidharta, 1983).

Psychological Feelings in Architecture
Architecture is unique in creativity and art, and must always reflect the era and cultural back-
ground that produced it (Mortice, 2019).Architectural psychology can perceive the significant
impact of the design environment on human experience and behavior, and help understand
the relationship between humans and human design and the impact of the environment (Abel,
2021). The connection and exchange between the architectural plan and human brain psychol-
ogy are noteworthy (Alharbi & Basaad, 2022). Different buildings can generate different psy-
chological feelings. Each building will generate different spaces, each building also consists
of various spaces, and each space can give people different feeling (Zhao, 2016). The relation
between the design of architectural space and people’s psychology is complicated and subtle,
which are closely related to and mutually impact each other (Zhao, 2016).
Psychology and Behavior in Architecture
The mental and psychological effects of architectural frames on human beings have been
considered from the early shelters to today΄s modern structure. Since the human behavior is
performed in defined spaces, it is necessary to design the physical space based on people’s
behavioral characteristics (Tabaeian & Einifar, 2011).
1 3

1760 Journal of Psycholinguistic Research (2023) 52:1755–1784
The average person spends about 80–90% of their time indoors. Space, colors, aes-
thetics, materials, green design and acoustics are all engaging factors of design that play
a significant role in providing the user with a psychological experience, and designers
can enhance this experience (Bordwell, 2020). The space is infinite and shapeless, but
it is also ubiquitous. The space can be solid or virtual, which creates different psycho-
logical feelings through different forms. Different processing methods of location, form,
texture and color can cause different spatial magnitudes perceived by your mind (Zhao,
2016). During our daily lives, one is constantly moving in and out of various buildings
and the space you go through can always affect your moods. A dark unlighted area can
make you feel gloomy, whereas a well-lit and well-ventilated area can make you feel
welcome. Cramped and closed areas can promote a sense of claustrophobia, where large
open spaces give you the freedom to move about and feel free (e-architect, 2020).
The interplay between architectural design and human psychology is significant, yet
it remains largely unnoticed or even ignored both in and outside the design industry
(Ricci, 2018). In the past 40 years large strides have been made in understanding and
dealing with human behavior. A significant force has been the work of behavioral psy-
chologists, who utilize a natural science approach in their investigations. Their empha-
sis has been upon the observation and manipulation of behavior, rather than simply
“explaining” it through reference to entities whose existence is inferred and not sus-
ceptible to direct measurement (Skirvin & Berman, 1973). Behavioral psychologists
are interested in determining cause-and-effect relationships between human behaviors
and the environmental factors which modify, maintain or preclude these behaviors.
Their approach is empirical and inductive (Skirvin & Berman, 1973).the relationship
between design and psychology is not only consequential, it is bidirectional. On the one
hand, successful design has been shown to have clear psychological and physiological
impacts; on the other, psychology, human experience, and the function of our neurologi-
cal systems all play a significant role in what we perceive to be successful design (Ricci,
2018). The psychological attitude of a human is affected by the design of interior archi-
tecture through various aspects (Mahmoud, 2017).
The Characteristics of the Sound
Sound is the result of the transmission of physical vibrations in a material environment,
and any matter, depending on the conditions, will be able to become a source of sound. In
fact, the sound is the vibration of the sound source and then the movement of waves and
air pressure fluctuations from the transmitter to the receiver, and three attributes of loud-
ness, pitch, and timbre are used to distinguish sounds, and the pitch of the sound is directly
related to the sensitivity of the ear. Sounds above 65–80 dB can damage the ears and are
also related to mental health, stress, and personal tension (Egan, 1976). In addition, the
unwanted sound will have adverse effects on the human body and soul for a long time,
and when the number and types of unwanted transmitters in the environment increase,
noise pollution will be created (Hami & Khodayari, 2021). In 2011, a study attempted to
describe the ecology of noise reduction, which consists of 6 components: 1) measurement
and analysis of challenges; 2) spatio-temporal dynamics; 3) the relationship between noise
reduction and environmental variables; 4) the effect of humans on sound; 5) the effects of
sound on humans 6) the effects of sounds on the ecosystem (Pijanowski et al., 2011).

The Mental Effect of Sound
There are many sounds surrounding us and we always seek to hear pleasant and vital
sounds and avoid unpleasant and dangerous sounds. In general, it should be said that as we
move forward, humans pay more attention to the audition.
Knowledge of architecture or the same place takes place over time, and different indi-
viduals have different initial feelings about architecture, which was to satisfy the need,
while the sound makes its impact at the same moment and its modes may be different. In
architecture, we move in place, that is, our mental background creates memories for us in
the place so that the repetition of two identical places reminds us of our mental, historical,
and environmental contexts. But in sound, we also move in the dimension of time, mean-
ing that at a certain time, a person is affected by a certain kind of sound according to the
environment, history, and memories, and time is one of the elements creating the desired
sound. So both of these two arts eventually reach a kind of unity.
The Effect of the Desired Sound
Pleasant sounds and music can affect brain activity. Music contains energy that, in addi-
tion to stimulating the brain, can influence all parts of the body. But some types of music
are less effective in stimulating the brain or completely ineffective. The reason for this can
be attributed to the complex structure of the brain and the diversity of human interests and

behaviors. In music, the structure of the human brain determines which type of music can
reduce humans’ harmful biological activities. Due to the complex structure of the human
brain, a specific type of music cannot have the same effect on all people. For many people,
pianissimo can be effective in creating relaxation. Music is effective in creating coordina-
tion between the activities of the two cerebral hemispheres. In the human brain, there is a
center for receiving music, which is located right behind the forehead, and this is the same
point responsible for learning and expressing human emotions. For this reason, there is a
direct relationship between music and the control and expression of emotions. The positive
effects of sound and music are evident to all. This is approved by many previous studies
on the effectiveness of sound in the treatment of patients, reducing anxiety, creating peace,
enhancing life expectancy, raising awareness, etc. (Hosseini & Zadehmohammadi, 2021;
Aldridge, 1994; Amir, 1992; NAJAFI et al., 2018; Heidari & Shahbazi, 2013; Chang &
Chen, 2005; Dai et al., 2020; Nilsson, 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Bradt et al., 2013; Hamel,
2001; Chlan, 1998; Najafi Ghezeljeh, 2018; Chiang, 2012; Williamson, 1992; Afshar et al,
2016; Ghiasvandian et al., 2014).
Adverse Effects of the Sound
Noise pollution refers to the existence of additional and annoying sounds that can disturb
human activities (Senate Public Works Committee, 1972). Noise pollution has negative
effects on human health and comfort based on the source and distribution characteristics,
and it is classified into four categories based on the duration and extent of the impact: 1)
Physical effects such as ear damage; 2) Physiological effects, such as increase of blood
pressure, heart arrhythmia, and stomach ulcer; 3) psychological effects, sleepiness and
delayed sleep–wake, irritability, and stress; and 4) effect on work performance, such as
reducing productivity and wrong perception of what is heard (Evans & Hygge, 2007).
Research shows that noise has negative effects on mental and psychological health, and
environmental noise is considered a critical factor for urban health (Hami & Khodayari,
2021; Hong & Jeon, 2017).
Psychology of Spiritual Experience
Spirituality refers to “a sense of wonder and astonishment of the mystery of existence”
(Leicester, 2005; Leicester & Modgil, 2005). Spiritual awareness is basically achieved in
the form of emotion and passion. So, when it comes to it, it is expressed in the framework
of thought. Of course, if we believe that we can talk about such a state (Wright, 2003). In
addition to the emphasis on spiritual feelings, there is also the desire to not limit spiritual-
ity and spiritual experience to religious experience. Regarding spirituality, it is necessary
to pay attention to something beyond individual religiosity. Nowadays, psychology gives
great importance to spiritual experience and various research has been done in the field of
experiences of spiritual sense in different sciences. For example, one can refer to (Man-
sour, 2022; Murdoch & Davies, 2017; Birch & Sinclair, 2013; Carroll, 2003; Geva, 2012;
Matracchi & Sadeghi Habibabad, 2021; Kim et al., 2022; Anand, 2014; Rastogi et al.,
2018; Kumar et al., 2020; Aftanas & Golocheikine, 2002; Kakumanu et al., 2018).
Islam is undoubtedly one of the divine religions and according to its followers, it is the
last program sent by God to His servants. The design and structure of this religion are such

Introduction of the Case Study (Nasir al‑Mulk Mosque, Shiraz)
The Nasir al-Molk Mosque is one of the most beautiful mosques in Shiraz city, Iran. It is
located in God-e Araban neighborhood and on Lotfali Khan Zand Street, near the famous
Shah Cheragh Mosque. This mosque is one of the Qajar buildings. This mosque has a large
courtyard in the center of which there is a large pond with a length of 16.5 m and a width
of 4.5 m. The Morvarid vault is located on the northern side of the courtyard, a Shabi-
stan with 7 stone columns on its eastern side, two minarets on its southern side, and the
main Shabistan with stained glass windows on its western side. Also, the mosque has two
porches (Ghochani & Mousavi, 2022) (Fig. 1)
The Nasir al-Mulk Mosque (1293 –1305 A.H.) was built on the “Lotfali Khan Zand”
Street by the order of “Mirza Hasan Ali Khan” nicknamed “Nasir al-Mulk” who was one
of the nobles of Shiraz. Its architects were “Mohammed Hasan Memar” and “Mohammed
Reza Kashipaz” (Parsaei et al., 2009). This mosque is next to Haji Nasir al-Mulk’s house
in “Ishaq Beig” neighborhood (Hussaini Fasāʾī, 1988) (Zarei & Razani, 2020) (Figs. 2, 3).
Western Shabistan
The most important part of this Shabistan includes seven wooden doors that connect it
to the courtyard of the mosque. These seven doors are decorated with eye-catching girih
tiles and Ghavareh bori, using stained glass. The juxtaposition of glasses with cold and
warm colors has brought special beauty to this original and unique composition. These
seven doors have an altar frame with a deliberate axis of symmetry, and the cornices are

Method
The approach followed in this research is a combination of descriptive-analytical, survey,
and laboratory methods, which is discussed below:
– First part:
In this part, the author has categorized the components and characteristics related to
sound by using the available reliable sources on the research topic, and then, the concep-
tual research model was presented. Then, using a questionnaire and selecting a statistical
1 3

1766 Journal of Psycholinguistic Research (2023) 52:1755–1784
Fig. 4 The spiritual space of the main Shabistan of Nasir al-Mulk Mosque, Shiraz, Iran
population of experts with a sample size of 64 people, the research hypotheses were tested
in the SPSS software and the components were ranked using Friedman’s test. The samples
were selected using the “virtual snowball” sampling method and a population of experts,
including professors and Ph.D. researchers of specialized fields of Islamic architectural
engineering and acoustics, was selected. The questionnaire was sent online to experts via
email.
– Second part:
In this part, 6 sound pressure levels, from 30 to 80 dB, of the sound used in the research,
i.e. “Adhan” (End Note 2) sound, were adjusted and prepared (Fig. 5), and then, played to
the subjects through headphones in the next step. The reason for choosing the sound pres-
sure level among the sound characteristics was the results of the experts’ answers to the
questions, according to which sound pressure level was ranked first in the previous part.
Also, the photo of the Shabistan of Nasir al-Mulk Mosque was taken using a special cam-
era, and a 360-degree photo of it was prepared to be used in virtual reality glasses.
– Third part:
In this part, the statistical sample size was estimated to be 23 people who were selected
by the “convenience sampling” method. 23 people (14 men—9 women) aged 17 to 39 years
old came to the EEG laboratory for testing. A week was required to conduct the test and
record all the data carefully. To do the test, the users (End Note 1) were asked to sit in a
chair that was prepared in advance and see the 360-degree image of Nasir al-Mulk Mosque
in Shiraz through virtual reality glasses (Fig. 6), then through a special cap used for record-
ing brain waves, their brain waves were recorded.
The inclusion criteria were to complete the consent form and fill out the general health
questionnaire. The test was performed in several steps: 1- The brain waves of the users were
recorded to investigate the normal test; 2- The images of the mosque were shown to the users
and their brain waves were recorded again when they saw the space of the mosque; 3- In the
main part of the test, through the headphones, the different intensities of the sound that had
been prepared in advance were played for the users, and the effects of six sound pressure levels

Data Analysis
First part: After receiving online questionnaires from experts and removing some incom-
plete questionnaires, 64 questionnaires filled out by the population of experts were ana-
lyzed. (Table 4) shows the characteristics of the samples:
To investigate the results, the collected data were entered into the SPSS software. Fried-
man’s test was used to rank the characteristics.
To validate the questionnaire, the reliability of the questionnaire was estimated by
Cronbach’s alpha. Since it is obtained to be above 0.7, the questionnaire has acceptable
reliability (Table5). Also, to determine the content validity of the questionnaire, it was
reviewed by several experts in this field, and their suggestions were used, and repetitive
and meaningless questions were removed from the questionnaire.

The results of Friedman’s test showed that among the characteristics of sound that
are effective in creating/enhancing the spiritual sense in the architecture of mosques,
sound pressure level obtains the highest score, followed by sound concept, the ampli-
tude of sound, sound quality, sound source, and sound type, respectively (Table6).
Second and third parts: in the brain wave recording laboratory, the prepared images
of the Nasir al-Mulk mosque, Shiraz were shown to 23 subjects, who were selected by
the “convenience sampling” method, through virtual reality glasses and the selected
sound was played for them through headphones. Next, using an EEG headset with elec-
trode positions in 10/20 system, the data related to the effect of image and sound on the
subjects’ minds were recorded. After placing a special headset on the subject’s head, a
special gel was injected under the electrodes to establish a current between the scalp and
the electrodes. Ambient temperature and annoying noises were controlled in the labora-
tory environment. Brain waves were recorded using a device manufactured by the medi-
com co., Russia. To this end, according to the studies by (Cahn & Polich, 2006; Essawy
et al., 2014; Frescura et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2020; Lubar, 1991), alpha waves and
theta/beta ratio were measured. In this way, with the increase of the alpha wave and the
decrease of the theta/beta ratio, it can be concluded that the users have reached tran-
quility and a spiritual sense. Figures 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 show the values of the
alpha wave and the theta/beta ratio for the test steps. The results show that 40 dB is the
most effective sound pressure level in promoting/creating a spiritual sense in the Nasir
al-Mulk Mosque, followed by sound pressure levels of 50, and 30 dB, respectively.
It should also be noted that the sound pressure levels (ranging from 60 to 80 dB and
above) have the opposite effect in creating/enhancing the spiritual sense. They reduce
the spiritual sense.

Conclusion
The study of the effect of Sound on the religious places regarding improving the interior qual-
ity of architecture is necessary because the mysterious manifestation of Sound in the wor-
ship spaces of mosques has created a dramatic change in place and has increased the spiritual
1 3

Journal of Psycholinguistic Research (2023) 52:1755–1784 1777
quality of these spaces. However, in contemporary religious places, the use of Sound has been
reduced to mere quantitative use, and the use of its qualitative aspects has been neglected.
Therefore, it is required to consider it in the architectural design of religious places.
Sound is one of the most beautiful gifts from God, so every sound should include God-
seeking goodness so that it can be useful for its listeners. Perhaps, this goodness can be
explored in how sound is manifested, which is a truth in meaning, in Islamic architecture. Ira-
nian architecture also has this goodness in its body and aims to bring benefits to human beings.
In Islamic architecture, the mosque, as the most important manifestation of Islamic
architecture, has been considered a spiritual environment from the beginning until now.
It is important to pay attention to spiritual features in the architecture of such buildings.
Considering sensory patterns in the design of the constituent elements of mosques has
increased spatial desirability, leading to the creation and strengthening of adaptive sensory
architectural patterns in religious places.
The mosque is considered a material body and it was created to facilitate such a spir-
itual event for a person. Undoubtedly, the nature of such materiality, unlike other earthy
materiality, should include a spiritual atmosphere, and it should depict a world other than
the world of sense using some qualities. Such materiality must be full of symbols and sym-
bolic signs that make a person suddenly remember a world other than his current world.
Although the appearance of the materials in this world is solid, rough, and hard, their
inside, which is the truth of an object, is soft, bright, and transparent and belongs to the
metamaterial world, and the designer of mosques in the Islamic era tried to show the truth
of the inside of these materials by unfolding the appearance of these materials.
The results of the first part of the research showed that the most effective characteristics
of sound in creating/enhancing the spiritual sense in the architecture of mosques, accord-
ing to the experts, is sound intensity, followed by sound concept, the amplitude of sound,
sound quality, sound source, and sound type. Also, the results of the analysis of users’ brain
waves in the second part of the research show that sound intensity (40–45 dB) is the most
effective intensity in creating/enhancing a spiritual sense feeling in Nasir al-Mulk Mosque,
Shiraz. As the sound intensity rises above (50 dB), the tranquility and spiritual sense in
the Shabistan of Nasir al-Mulk Mosque decrease. The importance of sensory indicators in
reducing or improving the quality of the environment can be clearly seen and neglecting
them can result in the reduced quality of architecture. It is suggested to investigate other
characteristics of sound in future studies and to analyze the effects of each on the minds of
the users of Islamic spaces etc. Obviously, the more we move away from the virtual space
and enter the real space of architecture, the more accurate and scientific the results will be.
The limitations of the present research did not allow the tests to be carried out in the real
environment of the Nasir al-Mulk Mosque, and we had to use virtual reality.
